what_it_does: Quantum computers make errors at a rate that makes useful computation impossible without error correction. The dominant error-correction strategy — surface codes — works by encoding one reliable logical qubit into a grid of many physical qubits, and the grid must grow quadratically as you want to correct more errors, making very large systems impractically expensive in physical qubits. A newer family called quantum LDPC (Low-Density Parity-Check) codes offers far better error-correction scaling (fewer physical qubits per logical qubit) but cannot, on their own, support the full set of operations needed for universal quantum computation. HetEC proposes a computer architecture that uses both code families together in a heterogeneous (mixed) design: LDPC code regions store most logical qubits efficiently, while surface code regions handle the specific gate operations that LDPC codes struggle with, including a process called magic state distillation that is required for certain universal gates. The paper defines the hardware interfaces and protocols needed to move logical qubits and perform gate operations across the boundary between the two code types.
